newsitem.title: MEXICO: Volcano spews ash over Mexico City, confusion mounts.
newsitem.headline: Volcano spews ash over Mexico City, confusion mounts.

text.p: Mexico's towering Popocatepetl volcano spewed a giant cloud of ash over the Mexico City metropolis on Monday, but emergency officials gave confused reports about the level of danger.

At a hastily called news conference in the capital, Interior Ministry officials denied that they issued a red alert on the volcano, although high-ranking government officials had previously broadcast the warning on national television.

In state capitals on the fringes of the 17,890-foot-high (5,500 metres) Popocatepetl, officials said the red alert had been reduced to a yellow warning as the intense activity died down on Monday night.
"There was confusion. There never was a red alert," Ricardo Garcia Villalobos, undersecretary for civil protection at the Interior Ministry, told the news conference.
A red alert is the highest warning signal for volcanoes in Mexico. It means the volcano is becoming unstable.

The muddle among emergency officials mirrored fear and confusion among many of the 18 million inhabitants of Mexico City, who were surprised by blankets of black ash, sodden with rain, falling across the giant metropolitan area.

The sand-like ash clogged car windscreens on streets from Mexico City's north to south, and nervous drivers waited in traffic jams. Radio stations urged extreme caution among drivers because of slippery roads and lack of visibility.

Alfredo Elias Ayud, Mexico's airport chief, told Radio Red that the capital's international airport had been temporarily shut down because of the ash, and flights were diverted to the Pacific resort of Acapulco in southwestern Mexico.
Mexico City residents in different parts of the metropolis complained of burning eyes and an acrid smell of sulphur. Some students were given face masks as they left evening classes.
Mexico City lies some 33 miles (50 kms) northwest of Popocatepetl, which officials said was hit by its most intense seismic disruption since 1925 at around 5:55 pm (6:55 p.m. EDT /2255 GMT).
The jolts sent a cloud of ash that blew as far as Veracruz, a port some 180 miles (290 km) to its east.

Burning rocks rained down the volcano's flanks, and troops and other rescue personnel were rushed to 30 villages containing thousands of citizens at the base of Popocatepetl to begin preparations for evacuation.

The last time locals were ordered to leave homes near the volcano was in December 1994 -- a decision that was widely resented when locals returned home after days in government shelters to find their houses burgled and their farm animals dying of starvation.
Officials said Popocatepetl's activity was worse than in 1994, but they decided against evacuation at the last minute.
"An evacuation means moving people from their homes and that bothers them and causes unnecessary problems," Agustin Gasca, an emergency official, told reporters.

Popocatepetl stands on the border of three states -- Puebla, Morelos and Mexico -- and tens of thousands of people live at the foot of its southeastern flanks, potentially in striking distance if it blows.

"We've warned local officials that we have emergency personnel and soldiers in position and ready for evacuation if that is what is decided," Manuel Bartlett Diaz, governor of the southeastern state of Puebla, told Televisa television.
Popocatepetl has spewed out ash and steam on numerous occasions this year, but officials had insisted it remained fundamentally stable.
